body: On a Saturday morning a man of thirty-eight is driving to the tip with a boot full of the previous tenant’s rubbish, and his route takes him past a car park that is full. It is full because of the building next to it, which he was inside most weeks for about nineteen years. He does not slow down. He notices the cars, and then he notices himself noticing the cars, and then he is at the lights and thinking about whether the tip takes paint. On the way back the car park is emptying and there are people standing about in it talking, and he takes the other road, which is longer, and he could not tell you why he did that.

That is an ordinary morning and it does not need explaining. Something went past him that he was not expecting to feel anything about, and he did feel something, and it was gone by the time he got home.

If you have not been inside a church in a while, you probably already know the shape of what usually gets said next, and you can feel it coming from the first sentence. This is not that, and you can stop reading the moment it starts to be.

The phrase stopped going is worth taking at face value, because almost nobody does. Going is a thing you do with your body: you get in a car at a fixed hour on a fixed day and you walk through a door where people will see you and speak to you. Stopping that is a decision about a building, a diary and a set of faces. It is not the same event as deciding that none of it is true, and yet the two are treated as one thing constantly, which is why so much of what gets said to people in this position lands as an accusation about their beliefs when the actual obstacle was a door.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. Several of them are hosted for the long night and the hours when nobody is up, and they run whether or not anybody has tuned in.

Those frequencies are programmed on a rule that costs something to keep: nothing on them asks the listener for a decision. There is no appeal at the end of the hour, no moment where the music stops and a voice explains what you should now do about it, and nobody at this end is counting who came back. That is a real cost, because it means never finding out whether any of it did anything, which is the sort of feedback most organisations cannot live without. It is given up on purpose. You do not have to have worked out what you believe before you are allowed to listen to something.

The usual approach fails for a reason worth naming plainly. People left for entirely different reasons — some because of something that was done to them, and done to them there; some drifted and could not tell you which year it happened; some still hold most of it and cannot face the room. Those are three unrelated situations, almost always addressed as one, in the same warm tone, with the same invitation attached at the end. A person in the first group hears that invitation coming from a long way off, and it confirms what they already suspected: that the interest was in getting them through the door.

So it is worth knowing how the dial is laid out, since the difference matters here. There are frequencies where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through, and if that is what you want, they are there and easy to find. There are also frequencies where nobody talks at all — hours of music with no host between the tracks, no appeal and no application. You are not obliged to start at the talking end, and nothing on this band moves you towards it.
None of this is an argument against churches. It would be a strange argument for a Christian radio ministry to make.

So be fair to the building first, because it does what no signal can. A congregation can bring food to a house, sit through a funeral, notice a chair empty for three weeks and go and find out why. It baptises, it marries, it buries, and it holds people by their name and their history rather than as an anonymous listener. Nothing here replaces that or is trying to. But a building has an hour, and a door, and a room of people who look up when it opens — and for anyone for whom the door is the whole difficulty, every good thing inside it sits on the far side of the one thing they cannot do.
A door has an hour. A frequency does not.

At three in the morning a woman in her fifties is in a relatives’ room on the fourth floor with her father’s coat folded on her lap because there was nowhere else to put it. She has not been inside a building like that in eleven years and has her reasons, and they are good ones. The television in the corner is showing a property programme with the sound off. She puts her phone face down on the arm of the chair with something playing very quietly, because the room has a hum in it she cannot listen to any more. She does not pray. Somewhere in the third hour a tune goes past that she knew every word of when she was fifteen, and she does not turn it off, and that is all that happens.
Nobody addressed her and nothing was asked of her. She had a bad night in a hard chair, and it was not a silent one.

It has to be said plainly that this is not much. A radio band cannot sit with you, cannot bring anything round, and does not know your name or what happened. If what you needed was for somebody to notice you had gone and come and find you, a frequency is not that. Nothing on this dial can undo what was done to somebody in a church, and it would be an insult to suggest a well-chosen station is any kind of answer to it.

But small and honest is a better offer than large and conditional. What is here costs you nothing you are not willing to spend — no room to walk into, nobody to explain yourself to, no conversation about where you have been. It can simply be on, in the car and the kitchen and the bad hour at three in the morning, for as long as that is all you want from it. Whatever you eventually conclude about any of it, you will not have had to work it out in silence, and nothing had to be declared first to be allowed the company.

That is the whole of it. There is no argument in this article that you are supposed to be persuaded by, because being persuaded is not the point and would not help. There is a frequency, it plays continuously, and you can leave it on without joining anything or telling anybody. You do not have to have worked out what you believe before you are allowed to listen to something true.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial. Most of the band is music — worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them. You can turn through all four and stop wherever you like, and nothing on the band requires you to have made your mind up about anything.

If you want somewhere to start, HM 314.40 — Midnight Praise — is probably the one. It is Celtic and European ambient worship, contemplative and largely wordless in feel, made by Nova Inspire for the long night, the overnight watch and the ones still awake. Nobody talks between the tracks, and nothing at the end of the hour asks you for anything. It suits the kitchen at two in the morning, the drive home, the hard chair on the fourth floor, and it keeps going whether you are listening closely, half listening, or have left the room. If it is not what you want, another frequency may be, and it costs nothing to turn the dial past this one.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else. There is an account, and what it does is keep your favourites with you across the Jubilee sites and show the band which frequencies people reach for, which is how the next station gets chosen. It will keep. Nobody is going to write to you about it.

So that is all, and there is genuinely nothing after this paragraph. If you put HM 314.40 on tonight, nothing follows from it: no one will ring you, no one will turn up, and there is no next step waiting further down the page. If you turn it off after four minutes, that is fine too, and nothing here will notice or mind. It is simply something true, playing, in the hours when the house is quiet — and it will be there at that number whenever you happen to want it, this week or in ten years, without anybody having asked you for a thing.
